summary: Defines a MIB module for managing Very High Speed Digital Subscriber Line (VDSL) interfaces. A MIB is a set of objects that network management protocols like SNMP can read and configure. This one covers VDSL line settings and status.

eli5.summary: A MIB is like a dashboard of dials and switches for a device. This one is the dashboard for fast home internet lines that run over phone wire.

questions: how to manage vdsl lines with snmp
what is a vtuc and vtur
what interface types does the vdsl mib use
subtitle: The SNMP management objects for VDSL lines: settings, status, error counters, profiles and alarms.

tldr.problem: Operators who run Very High Speed Digital Subscriber Line (VDSL) equipment need a standard way to configure lines and read their status and error statistics over SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the VDSL-LINE-MIB module, which hooks into the Interfaces MIB, splits each line into a central (Vtuc) and a remote (Vtur) transceiver, keeps counters in 15-minute and 1-day buckets, and shares settings through configuration profiles.
tldr.outcome: VDSL interfaces can be provisioned and monitored with one common object set, with threshold notifications for line problems. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 3728 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the VDSL-LINE-MIB module for SNMP management of VDSL lines.

sections.title: What the VDSL Line MIB Covers
sections.content:
This RFC defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for managing VDSL lines. MIB objects are normally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and are written in the SMIv2 language described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580. The framework overview is in RFC 3410.

The definitions are based on VDSL specifications from T1E1, ETSI and ITU documents. The module sits in the MIB tree under the MIB-2 transmission branch, as vdslMIB number 97.
sections.eli5: A MIB is a big list of the things a device can tell you and the things you can change on it. This one is the list for fast phone-wire internet.

sections.title: Fitting Into the Interfaces MIB
sections.content:
A VDSL line is a data interface, so the MIB integrates with the Interfaces Group MIB of RFC 2863. IANA assigned three interface types: vdsl(97) for the line, and interleave(124) and fast(125) for the optional interleaved and fast channels.

Most tables extend ifEntry and are indexed by ifIndex, and those entries MUST be persistent. Standard interface attributes such as ifIndex, ifType and ifOperStatus are not duplicated. The RFC adds a few rules: ifPhysAddress MUST be an octet string of zero length, and ifLinkUpDownTrapEnable defaults to enabled(1).

The MIB has two groups: vdslGroup (line-code independent objects) and vdslNotificationGroup. Line, physical, performance and profile tables belong to the vdsl(97) interface. Channel tables belong to the interleave(124) and fast(125) interfaces. For VDSL lines, both groups are mandatory.
sections.eli5: Each line gets a numbered slot in the device's list of network connections. This MIB adds extra pages of details to that slot instead of repeating what is already there.

sections.title: Line Topology and Naming
sections.content:
A VDSL line has two ends. The Vtuc is the transceiver at the central (network side) end, and the Vtur is the transceiver at the remote (customer side) end. A Vtu is either one. The MIB defines a VdslLineEntity convention for the two sides, with vtuc(1) and vtur(2).

A second convention, VdslLineCodingType, identifies the line coding: other(1), mcm(2) for Multiple Carrier Modulation, or scm(3) for Single Carrier Modulation.

Object names use short abbreviations, such as Atn for attenuation, Snr for signal to noise ratio, Mgn for margin, Psd for power spectral density, ES, SES and UAS for errored, severely errored and unavailable seconds, and Lof, Los, Lpr and Lol for loss of frame, signal, power and link.
sections.eli5: A line has a box at the phone company end and a box at the customer end. The MIB keeps track of both boxes and uses short nicknames for the measurements.

sections.title: Counters, Buckets and Profiles
sections.content:
For loss of frame, link, signal and power, and for errored, severely errored and unavailable seconds, the MIB keeps event counters, a current 15-minute bucket, 0 to 96 history buckets of 15 minutes, and 0 to 30 history buckets of one day. They use the 64-bit textual conventions of RFC 3705, which extend RFC 3593. There is no required alignment between a 15-minute interval and the wall clock. Counters are not reset when a Vtu is reinitialized, only when the agent is reset or reinitialized.

Because a managed node can handle hundreds or thousands of lines, most of which are set up identically, the MIB uses profiles: sets of parameters shared by many lines. There are line configuration profiles and alarm configuration profiles. If a profile changes, every line that refers to it is reconfigured, and a profile must be unreferenced from all lines before it is deleted.

Implementations MUST provide a default profile named DEFVAL for each profile type, with vendor-specific values unless stated otherwise. Profile changes MUST take effect immediately and MAY restart the units on the line. All read-write and read-create objects SHOULD be stored persistently.
sections.eli5: The device keeps a scoreboard of problems for each 15-minute stretch and each day. Instead of setting up thousands of lines one by one, you write a recipe card once and point many lines at it.

sections.title: Notifications and Thresholds
sections.content:
Agents are required to be able to generate the SNMP coldStart/warmStart notifications (per RFC 3418) and linkUp/linkDown (per RFC 2863). The MIB itself adds notifications for initialization failure and for threshold crossings on lof, lol, los, lpr, ES, SES and UAS.

Each threshold has its own value, and a value of 0 disables that notification. A notification occurs when the current 15-minute counter becomes equal to or exceeds the threshold, and at most one may be sent per interval per interface. Since the counters reset every 15 minutes, a lasting condition can notify as often as every 15 minutes. Setting a threshold to 1 gives a notification whenever the event occurs, at most once every 15 minutes.

The object vdslPhysCurrStatus is a bitmask of outstanding error conditions on a transceiver. Remote status comes over the embedded operations channel (EOC), so it may be unavailable for units that cannot be reached during a line error.
sections.eli5: You can tell the device 'ring a bell if more than this many problems happen in 15 minutes'. Setting the number to zero turns that bell off.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with read-write or read-create access may be sensitive, and SET operations without protection can harm network operations. Some readable objects are also sensitive. The RFC points out that a subscriber with VDSL layer connectivity from the Vtur can manipulate the link and the EOC for their own loop, so unfiltered fluctuations could generate enough notifications to overwhelm the management interface or element manager. Write access to configuration could also let an end user raise their service level or affect other users.

The line, line configuration and alarm configuration tables are treated as sensitive. So are the performance tables, because low utilization at certain times of day might indicate an empty office or residence.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC RECOMMENDS the SNMPv3 security features, including its authentication and privacy mechanisms, and says deploying earlier SNMP versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators remain responsible for giving access only to legitimate principals.
sections.eli5: Some dials could be used to cheat or snoop, and even usage patterns can show when nobody is home. So only the right people should be allowed to look at or turn them, and the messages should be protected.
